# Session 12: Sample & QC

## 📋 Agenda

Hands on keyboards. Your track, your data.

- **20 min** — sample a balanced subset, create the annotation sheet
- **25 min** — annotate **blind**, two of you, independently
- **25 min** — agreement → disagreements → adjudicate
- **10 min** — a baseline prompt, small

::: {.callout-important}
`PLAN.md` signed first. Steps 1–2 need no model, so nothing is blocked while you wait.
:::

## 🎯 Learning Objectives {.smaller}

By the end of this session, you will be able to:

- Draw a **balanced** subset and explain why balance matters for P/R/F1 and the matrix.
- Annotate independently and blind, and interpret your percent agreement and Cohen's κ.
- Adjudicate disagreements into one agreed gold set, and record **what changed**.
- Get a baseline number to beat.

# Step 1 — Sample

## Pool vs. sample

A **pool** is everything the corpus has, with its natural imbalance:

```
cefr_pool.json → A1: 51 · A2: 246 · B1: 1229 · B2: 1188 · C1: 436 · C2: 33
```

. . .

A **sample** is what you study — equal items per label:

```{.python}
sampled = sample_pool(pool, N_PER_CLASS, SEED)
# Sampled 42 items. Per-label counts: {'A1': 7, 'A2': 7, ... 'C2': 7}
```

## Why balance

With 1229 B1s and 33 C2s, a model that answers "B1" to everything scores well on accuracy and tells you nothing.

Balanced sampling makes **per-class** precision and recall readable, and makes the confusion matrix a picture of *what gets confused with what* rather than a picture of the class sizes.

. . .

::: {.callout-note}
Rare classes simply yield fewer — that is a property of the data, and it belongs in your limitations section.
:::

## Why keep the pool separate

The items you *didn't* sample have a job: they become your **few-shot examples** in step 4.

If your examples came from your gold set, you would be showing the model the answers you are about to test it on.

. . .

`build_fewshot` avoids this for you — but only if there is a pool left to draw from. Sample from the **full pool**, not the demo file.

# Step 2 — QC

## The part no model can do

The published labels are somebody else's judgment.

. . .

Before you measure a model against them, **two of you** re-annotate the sample independently and blind. Then you find out how far apart you were. Then you argue.

. . .

This is the same A–F round-trip you did by hand in **Session 5** — now on your own track.

## Blind means blind

`create_annotation_sheet` deliberately does **not** copy the published label across.

```
| ID | Text                          | CoderA | CoderB | Final | Note |
|----|-------------------------------|--------|--------|-------|------|
| 1  | Bears do not have good hearing|        |        |       |      |
```

. . .

CoderA and CoderB fill their own columns without looking at each other's. `Final` stays empty until you have talked.

::: {.callout-tip}
The Sheet is a real Google Sheet — everyone can work in it at once. It is the one part of the repo that is genuinely concurrent.
:::

## Then measure

```{.python}
rows = load_annotation_sheet(SHEET_ID, ROUND)
annotator_agreement(rows)
# 42 doubly-annotated · agreement 71.4% · Cohen's kappa 0.657
disagreements(rows)
# 12 rows to adjudicate.
```

. . .

**Write those two numbers down.** They go in report section 1, and they are the evidence that the QC pass happened.

## Adjudicate

The 12 rows you disagreed on are not noise. They are the places where **your scheme is unclear** — and they are the same places the model will struggle.

. . .

For each: agree a `Final` label, and note *why*. Then:

```{.python}
gold = to_canonical(rows, LABELS)
compare_to_published(gold, sampled)
# 37 / 42 match the published label (88.1%)
```

. . .

Those 5 differences are a finding about the corpus, not a mistake by you.

## The consequence

::: {.callout-important}
## Your adjudicated gold is what the model gets scored against
Not the published labels.
:::

That is what makes this session load-bearing. The boundaries you argue about here are the ones you will point at on Day 5 when you explain why the model missed something.

# Step 3 — Baseline

## Small, on purpose

```{.python}
f1_by_round = {}
PROMPT = load_prompt(PROMPT_FILE)
pred0 = run_prompt(PROMPT, gold)
f1_by_round["0 zero-shot"] = evaluate(gold, pred0, ordered=True)
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Keep `N_PER_CLASS = 2` for now
One full-size round is ~40 model calls and **≥3 minutes of enforced pacing**. The free tier gives you ~500 calls a day. Iterate small; save the full run for the one you freeze tomorrow.
:::

## Write the plainest prompt you can

Resist making it good.

The point of a baseline is that later rounds have something to be measured **against** — and that you find out what the model does with no help at all.

. . .

A baseline that is already tuned tells you nothing about whether your tuning worked.
